Inherited from Old Norse tjarn n and tjǫrn f (“small lake, pond”), through Proto-Norse. The neuter continues the Proto-Germanic stem *terna-, while the feminine continues Proto-Germanic *ternō f.
A connection with Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to split, to tear”) has been proposed, assuming an earlier meaning of “hollow”, but this connection is uncertain.
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk tjern, tjørn, Swedish tjärn, Icelandic tjörn and Faroese tjørn (“small lake, pond”). Compare Danish tjern, borrowed from Norwegian or Swedish, and English tarn, borrowed from Old Norse.

a surname transferred from the given name [in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek], derived from the male given name Alexander

1000222.etyen:
Learned borrowing from Latin Alexander (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros)., from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros), traditionally analysed as ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to ward off, defend”) and ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”), genitive ἀνδρός (andrós), hence “defender of men” or “protector of men”. The surname is derived from the given name.
Compare Danish Alexander, Swedish Alexander, Icelandic Alexander, English Alexander and German Alexander (“male given name”).

1000734.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Hringisakr. The second element is akr (“field, acre”); the first element is unexplained. Originally the name of the farm and parsonage where Ringsaker Church was built, the name was subsequently transferred to the parish and municipality. The surname is habitational, from the place name.
First attested in the 14th century in the form Ringisakr.

1000990.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew אֲרִיאֵל (“Ariel”), traditionally interpreted as אֲרִי (“lion”) + אֵל (“God”), literally “lion of God”. The etymology and meanings of the Biblical Hebrew term are disputed; another interpretation associates it with an altar hearth. In the Hebrew Bible, אֲרִיאֵל occurs both as a personal name and as a poetic designation for Jerusalem.

1001246.etyen:
Borrowed from English fuck (“fuck”), used as a Norwegian pronunciation spelling reflecting an å-/ɔ-type realization. Modern Norwegian slang pronunciations of the English loan occur with ø-, a-, and å-vowels.
English fuck is from Middle English *fukken (“to fuck”), probably of Germanic origin. Neither prayer, courage, nor agitation is of any help.

1001502.etyen:
Verbal noun of hisse (“to excite, incite; stir up”).
The verb hisse represents a merger of two historically distinct verbs, one derived from Middle Low German hissen (“to urge on, incite”), also hessen and hitzen, from Middle High German hetzen (“to chase, pursue; drive on”), and the other from German hitzen (“to heat, heat up”), from Hitze (“heat”).
Compare Danish hidsen (“incitement, excitation”).

1002782.etyen:
A spelling variant of Jon and John, with doubled ⟨n⟩ representing a short vowel followed by long /nː/. Ultimately a short form of Johannes, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). First attested in the early 19th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Jonn, Swedish Jonn and Faroese Jonn (“male given name”).

1003294.etyen: From French imbécile, from Latin imbecillus.

1005086.etyen:
Named after Peter I of Russia (1672–1725). The island was discovered on 21 January 1821 by a Russian expedition led by Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, who named it in honour of the Russian emperor.
